rationale: A wins by a nose because it is meaner about proof and failure modes: "Do not pitch this without the harness" is the right posture for an unreproduced benchmark claim. B is cleaner on grounding, especially when it says "A bare number is a topic, not a story," but its "Next step: `journalist-fit-check`" moves too fast when the eval harness and customer access still decide whether the story exists. A has one overreaching angle; B has fewer mistakes but slightly less strategic utility.
gaps_in_A: "Two million models, and no easy way to know which ones are safe to use" turns a supplied scale fact into an asserted safety problem. Make it a question unless you have provenance, scanning, or buyer evidence.
"behind its own firewall" goes beyond the update. Private model hosting does not automatically mean customer-controlled firewall deployment.
"Hugging Face bets the next AI workload never leaves the device" overstates one on-device model release into a company-wide thesis.
"a commercial admission that pulling arbitrary weights is a governance problem" is a sharp inference, not a fact. It needs an enterprise buyer saying vetting drove the purchase.
gaps_in_B: "Next step: `journalist-fit-check`" is premature. The benchmark claim and customer story need fact-checking, eval configuration, and customer access first.
"A Fortune 100 manufacturer is paying Hugging Face to keep its models private" assumes payment and motive. The update only says the customer is cited for the enterprise tier.
"The prevailing belief is that reasoning quality tracks parameter count" imports outside context that was not supplied. It may be true enough, but it still needs support.
Rejecting "Hugging Face Hub passes 2 million models" is too blunt. The bare number is not a story, but provenance, auditability, and model-supply-chain risk could be one if properly caveated.
